motor_endplate_zones.method: modified Sihler's stain intramuscular nerve-dense region, with muscle-spindle abundance histology
motor_endplate_zones.notes: A notably PROXIMAL and compact nerve-dense region, about 2.88 cm2, in the upper fifth of the muscle -- nowhere near mid-belly. Highest spindle abundance in its upper third, at 11.33% of muscle length. The source's own paragraph on this muscle opens 'The FCR branch of the median nerve', which is a transcription slip: flexor carpi ulnaris is supplied by the ulnar nerve. The measurements match this muscle's rows in the paper's tables and are kept; the innervation statement is not.

ultrasound_injection_approach.transducer_placement: Transverse on the volar forearm, 3-4 cm distal to the elbow crease, on the ulnar side.
ultrasound_injection_approach.depth_layer: Most superficial on the ulnar side, lying over flexor digitorum profundus and the ulnar cortex.
ultrasound_injection_approach.identification_cues: Oval in cross-section. A 'cloud fascia' appearance marks its boundary.
ultrasound_injection_approach.notes: The strongest wrist flexor, and a principal contributor to the flexed-and-adducted wrist.
ultrasound_injection_approach.source: Diaconu S et al. (Elias University Hospital), 'A Visual Guide to Ultrasound-Guided Botulinum Toxin Injection in Spasticity: Part I -- Distal Upper Limb Muscles', Toxins 17(3):107 (2025), doi:10.3390/toxins17030107

trigger_points.location_description: Belly in the proximal third of the forearm along the ulnar border, a few centimetres distal to the medial epicondyle.
trigger_points.referred_pain_pattern: Ulnar side of the volar wrist around the pisiform, sometimes extending into the ulnar palm.
trigger_points.activation_perpetuating_factors: Forceful repetitive flexion-ulnar deviation (hammering, golf, casting, racquet sports), sustained gripping with a flexed wrist. Travell and Simons describe possible ulnar-nerve irritation by taut FCU bands at the elbow and forearm, producing ulnar paraesthesiae that resolve with trigger-point inactivation.
trigger_points.notes: Non-myofascial differential: ulnar neuropathy (cubital tunnel, Guyon's canal), pisotriquetral arthritis, hook of hamate fracture, TFCC injury, ulnar artery thrombosis, C8 radiculopathy.
trigger_points.source: Simons, Travell & Simons (1999) Trigger Point Manual, 2nd ed., Vol. 1, ch. 38; Donnelly et al. (2019) 3rd ed., ch. 38 -- as cited in this atlas's uploaded wrist muscle reference.

clinical.compiled_by: repository owner (physician); elbow_muscles_reference_v2.html, compiled 04/09/2026 (v2; v1 31/08/2026). Strength data come from the Mayo elbow series (An et al. 1981; Askew et al. 1987), from MRI/cadaver architecture studies (Murray et al. 2000; Kawakami et al. 1994) and from Neumann (2017). Values are population means; individual variation is large.
clinical.function_biomechanics: FCU flexes and ulnarly deviates the wrist (with ECU it is the ulnar-deviation couple used in hammering and the "dart-thrower's" motion) and fixes the pisiform so that abductor digiti minimi has a stable origin. Its elbow flexion moment is small. Its most important elbow role is dynamic valgus stabilisation: in cadaver loading with the ulnar collateral ligament sectioned, FCU alone produced the greatest correction of valgus angulation among the flexor–pronator muscles, FDS was second, pronator teres last; FCU+FDS co-contraction restored the most stability. Flexor–pronator conditioning is therefore central to protecting the ligament in overhead athletes.
clinical.adjacent_structures: Adjacent bursae: None named at the elbow. Adjacent structures and relations: Ulnar nerve (between the heads and then on the deep surface, with the ulnar artery joining it in the mid-forearm); at the wrist the ulnar nerve and artery lie lateral (radial) to the tendon; FDP deep; FDS lateral; the anterior band of the ulnar collateral ligament deep to the humeral head.

trigger_points.location: Proximal to mid forearm along the ulnar border, in the muscle belly a few centimetres distal to the medial epicondyle.
trigger_points.referred_pain: the ulnar side of the volar wrist (ulnar half of the wrist crease, pisiform region).
trigger_points.notes: Symptoms / mimics: Ulnar-sided wrist pain on gripping, ulnar deviation or leaning on the hand; confused with pisotriquetral arthritis, TFCC injury or ulnar neuropathy at the wrist. Entrapment: Tension in the FCU arcade compresses the ulnar nerve between the two heads (cubital tunnel syndrome): paraesthesia of the ring and little fingers, later intrinsic weakness; the ulnar nerve is also compressed proximally by the arcade of Struthers and the medial head of triceps, and distally by the deep flexor–pronator aponeurosis. Associated TrPs: FCR, FDS/FDP, palmaris longus, pronator teres, triceps medial head.
trigger_points.source: Travell & Simons, vol. 1, 2nd ed., 1999: ch. 38; ch. 33 pain guide.

clinical.pain_referred_into_territory: Pain referred INTO the medial elbow / ulnar forearm from elsewhere
clinical.notes: The FCU heads are the most common site of ulnar-nerve compression at the elbow; release includes Osborne's band and the FCU aponeurosis. The FCU fascicle of the ulnar nerve is a donor for nerve transfer to the biceps (Oberlin). Ulnar-sided origin pain is less common than PT–FCR pain in medial epicondylalgia.
clinical.caveat: Clinical reference for professional use; anatomical variation is frequent and trigger-point patterns describe typical, not universal, presentations. Referred pain is presented in both directions: pain that each muscle's TrPs refer to other regions, and pain that other muscles (shoulder, chest, back) and non-muscular sources refer into the elbow region. Where Travell & Simons did not map a muscle separately (extensor digiti minimi, pronator quadratus) this is stated rather than filled in.

clinical.compiled_by: repository owner (physician); wrist_muscles_reference_v2.html, compiled 31/08/2026. Sources. Gray's Anatomy 42nd ed. (2021) for attachments, innervation (root values as given by Gray's) and vascular supply; Travell, Simons & Simons' Trigger Point Manual, 2nd ed. (1999, Vol. 1) and 3rd ed. (2019) for trigger-point (TrP) locations and referred-pain patterns; Green's Operative Hand Surgery 8th ed. (2022) [4], Neumann (2017) [5], Kendall (2005) [6] and Kapandji (2019) [7] for kinesiology, Netter (2023) [54] for topographic cross-checking; and peer-reviewed primary literature for biomechanics, variants and clinical entities. Bracketed numbers point to the master list in Appendix B; every profile ends with its own reference list. Claims that could not be tied to a verified source are labelled [clinical reasoning] or [UNVERIFIED]. Appendix A grades the match between each key claim and its source.
clinical.function_biomechanics: Major: Wrist flexion; the pisiform lengthens its lever, and in cadaveric series FCU is the largest prime wrist flexor by PCSA and flexion moment arm [ranking grade B] [8, 10]. Its tendon shows the largest strain of the five prime motors under maximal predicted load (about 3.7%), a compliant, high-force design [11]. Minor: Ulnar deviation (with ECU forms the ulnar deviation couple used in hammering and casting); weak elbow flexion [1, 5]. Carpal stability: A carpal supinator with a protective role for the scapholunate joint (together with APL and ECRL); it also tensions the pisohamate and pisometacarpal ligaments that stabilize the ulnar carpus [14, 17]. Second-phase motor of the dart-throwing motion [19]. Importance: Power grip and ulnar-deviated wrist tasks. Transfer donor: FCU to ECRB (Green) in spastic wrist flexion; FCU to EDC in radial-nerve palsy; harvest sacrifices flexion–ulnar deviation power [4].
clinical.adjacent_structures: Bursae / sheaths: No synovial sheath (unique among the prime motors). The pisotriquetral joint, whose cavity often communicates with the radiocarpal joint, is the relevant closed space; Guyon's canal lies directly radial to the insertion [1, 4]. Coupled structures: Ulnar nerve (cubital tunnel proximally; Guyon's canal distally), pisiform and pisotriquetral joint, hook of hamate, TFCC-related ulnar column [1, 4, 27].

trigger_points.activation_perpetuating_factors: Forceful repetitive flexion–ulnar deviation (hammering, golf, casting, racquet sports), sustained gripping with a flexed wrist. Travell and Simons describe possible ulnar-nerve irritation by taut FCU bands at the elbow and forearm, producing ulnar paraesthesiae that resolve with TrP inactivation [grade B] [2, 3].

clinical.pain_referred_into_territory: Pain referred into FCU territory (ulnar volar wrist)
clinical.non_myofascial_differential: Ulnar neuropathy (cubital tunnel, Guyon's canal), pisotriquetral arthritis, hook of hamate fracture, TFCC injury, ulnar artery thrombosis, C8 radiculopathy.
clinical.notes: Cubital tunnel syndrome: the ulnar nerve is compressed under Osborne's ligament and between the FCU heads, where tunnel volume falls with elbow flexion; the FCU aponeurosis and deep flexor–pronator aponeurosis are decompression sites [27]. At the wrist the FCU tendon is the landmark for the ulnar neurovascular bundle (immediately radial to it) and forms the ulnar wall of Guyon's canal with the pisiform [4]. FCU tendinopathy and calcific tendinitis near the pisiform (the commonest site of calcific tendinitis at the wrist) and pisotriquetral arthritis all present as ulnar volar wrist pain [grade B].
clinical.caveat: Referred-pain maps from Travell and Simons are clinical consensus drawings, not experimentally derived; the APL and pronator quadratus maps (Hwang et al.) are experimental hypertonic-saline studies in healthy volunteers. Grade C items (Appendix A rows 23, 44–46, 48): TrP distances, muscle-level arterial detail, the ECRL/ECRB insertional bursa, the grip-strength claim for PL agenesis, and the extrapolated EDM/EPB/EPL referral statements. All are labelled in the text. Referred-pain conventions. "TrP referral" is the essential (dark) zone described by Travell and Simons unless "spillover" is stated. TrP locations in centimetres are approximations read from the Manual's figures and should be confirmed by palpation of the taut band. Quantitative biomechanical values are cadaveric means and vary with forearm rotation and wrist angle.
